manifest.title: Approximation algorithms

inputs.abstract:
We define optimization problems, $r$-approximation guarantees, independent
running-time guarantees, and L-reductions. PTAS, FPTAS, EPTAS, and QPTAS
combine correctness and time bounds on the same explicit program, with
ratio $1+\varepsilon$, where $\varepsilon=1/k$ and $k$ ranges over the
positive integers. Integer precision suffices for every positive real accuracy.
Instances and solutions are typed mathematical objects with fixed
representations. Programs use the archive's word-RAM semantics and may be
compiled from high-level implementations. Resource bounds control
instruction count and sufficient word width. This submission contains
definitions only.

concepts.title: Algorithm inputs
concepts.description:
An ordinary algorithm receives the instance's structural arena.
A scheme receives the arena of $(k,x)$, where the positive integer $k$
specifies accuracy $\varepsilon=1/k$. Only the integer is machine input.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.OptimizationProblem
import Lax560851.StructuralCombinators

/-!
---
title: Algorithm inputs
type: definition
---
An ordinary algorithm receives the instance's structural arena.
A scheme receives the arena of $(k,x)$, where the positive integer $k$
specifies accuracy $\varepsilon=1/k$. Only the integer is machine input.
-/

namespace Lax213208.AlgorithmInput

open OptimizationProblem
open Lax560851.WordArena Lax560851.StructuralCombinators

variable {Instance Solution : Type*}

def inputTape (problem : Problem Instance Solution)
    (precision : Option ℕ) (x : Instance) : List ℕ :=
  match precision with
  | none => inputWords problem x
  | some k => (encode (prod nat problem.input) (k, x)).toInput

end Lax213208.AlgorithmInput

concepts.title: Approximate and optimal solutions
concepts.description:
For $r\ge1$, an $r$-approximate solution is feasible and has value at most
$r\,\mathrm{OPT}$ for minimization, or at least $\mathrm{OPT}/r$ for
maximization. Comparison with every feasible solution avoids division by
zero and does not require an attained optimum.

An optimal value, when needed, is the value of an attained optimum.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.OptimizationProblem

/-!
---
title: Approximate and optimal solutions
type: definition
---
For $r\ge1$, an $r$-approximate solution is feasible and has value at most
$r\,\mathrm{OPT}$ for minimization, or at least $\mathrm{OPT}/r$ for
maximization. Comparison with every feasible solution avoids division by
zero and does not require an attained optimum.

An optimal value, when needed, is the value of an attained optimum.
-/

namespace Lax213208.Approximation

open OptimizationProblem

variable {Instance Solution : Type*}

def IsApproximation (problem : Problem Instance Solution)
    (r : ℝ) (x : Instance) (y : Solution) : Prop :=
  1 ≤ r ∧ problem.feasible x y ∧ ∀ z, problem.feasible x z →
    match problem.direction with
    | .minimize => (problem.value x y : ℝ) ≤ r * problem.value x z
    | .maximize => (problem.value x z : ℝ) ≤ r * problem.value x y

def IsOptimalValue (problem : Problem Instance Solution)
    (x : Instance) (value : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∃ y, IsApproximation problem 1 x y ∧ (problem.value x y : ℝ) = value

end Lax213208.Approximation

concepts.title: Efficient polynomial-time approximation schemes
concepts.description:
An EPTAS has ratio $1+\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon=1/k$, in time
$f(k)(n+2)^d$, where $f$ is computable and the exponent $d$ is
independent of precision.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.RApproximation
import Lax213208.RunningTime
import Mathlib.Computability.Partrec

/-!
---
title: Efficient polynomial-time approximation schemes
type: definition
---
An EPTAS has ratio $1+\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon=1/k$, in time
$f(k)(n+2)^d$, where $f$ is computable and the exponent $d$ is
independent of precision.
-/

namespace Lax213208.EPTAS

open OptimizationProblem Programs RApproximation RunningTime

variable {Instance Solution : Type*} {problem : Problem Instance Solution}

def EPTAS (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance) : Prop :=
  ∃ f : ℕ → ℕ, Computable f ∧ (∀ k > 0, 0 < f k) ∧
    ∃ d : ℕ, 0 < d ∧ ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k →
      let ε : ℝ := 1 / k
      Approximates (problem := problem) alg inputs (1 + ε) (some k) ∧
      RunsInTime (problem := problem) alg inputs
        (fun n => f k * (n + 2) ^ d) (some k)

end Lax213208.EPTAS

concepts.title: Fully polynomial-time approximation schemes
concepts.description:
An FPTAS has ratio $1+\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon=1/k$, in time
polynomial in both instance size and $k$. The constants and exponents
are independent of the instance and precision.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.RApproximation
import Lax213208.RunningTime

/-!
---
title: Fully polynomial-time approximation schemes
type: definition
---
An FPTAS has ratio $1+\varepsilon$, with $\varepsilon=1/k$, in time
polynomial in both instance size and $k$. The constants and exponents
are independent of the instance and precision.
-/

namespace Lax213208.FPTAS

open OptimizationProblem Programs RApproximation RunningTime

variable {Instance Solution : Type*} {problem : Problem Instance Solution}

def FPTAS (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance) : Prop :=
  ∃ c d e : ℕ, 0 < c ∧ 0 < d ∧ 0 < e ∧
    ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k →
      let ε : ℝ := 1 / k
      Approximates (problem := problem) alg inputs (1 + ε) (some k) ∧
      RunsInTime (problem := problem) alg inputs
        (fun n => c * (n + 2) ^ d * (k + 1) ^ e) (some k)

end Lax213208.FPTAS

concepts.title: L-reductions
concepts.description:
An L-reduction consists of polynomial-time instance and solution maps and
positive constants $a,b$. It maps valid instances and feasible solutions
to valid instances and feasible solutions, and satisfies
$\mathrm{OPT}_B(f(x))\le a\,\mathrm{OPT}_A(x)$ and
$|\mathrm{OPT}_A(x)-v_A(g(x,y))|
 \le b\,|\mathrm{OPT}_B(f(x))-v_B(y)|$.

Optima are required to be attained. The solution map receives both $x$
and $y$; its time is measured in their combined encoded size. Their word
lists are paired by prefixing the length of the first list.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.Approximation
import Lax213208.PolynomialComputation

/-!
---
title: L-reductions
type: definition
---
An L-reduction consists of polynomial-time instance and solution maps and
positive constants $a,b$. It maps valid instances and feasible solutions
to valid instances and feasible solutions, and satisfies
$\mathrm{OPT}_B(f(x))\le a\,\mathrm{OPT}_A(x)$ and
$|\mathrm{OPT}_A(x)-v_A(g(x,y))|
 \le b\,|\mathrm{OPT}_B(f(x))-v_B(y)|$.

Optima are required to be attained. The solution map receives both $x$
and $y$; its time is measured in their combined encoded size. Their word
lists are paired by prefixing the length of the first list.
-/

namespace Lax213208.LReduction

open OptimizationProblem Approximation PolynomialComputation

variable {SourceInstance SourceSolution TargetInstance TargetSolution : Type*}

def solutionMapInput (source : Problem SourceInstance SourceSolution)
    (target : Problem TargetInstance TargetSolution)
    (xy : SourceInstance × TargetSolution) : List ℕ :=
  let first := inputWords source xy.1
  first.length :: (first ++ target.output xy.2)

structure LReduction (source : Problem SourceInstance SourceSolution)
    (target : Problem TargetInstance TargetSolution)
    (sourceInputs : Set SourceInstance) (targetInputs : Set TargetInstance) where
  instanceMap : SourceInstance → TargetInstance
  solutionMap : SourceInstance → TargetSolution → SourceSolution
  optimumFactor : ℝ
  errorFactor : ℝ
  optimumFactor_pos : 0 < optimumFactor
  errorFactor_pos : 0 < errorFactor
  instanceMap_polytime :
    PolynomialTimeComputable (inputWords source) (inputWords target) instanceMap sourceInputs
  solutionMap_polytime :
    PolynomialTimeComputable (solutionMapInput source target) source.output
      (fun xy => solutionMap xy.1 xy.2)
      {xy | xy.1 ∈ sourceInputs ∧ target.feasible (instanceMap xy.1) xy.2}
  maps_instances : ∀ x ∈ sourceInputs, instanceMap x ∈ targetInputs
  maps_solutions : ∀ x ∈ sourceInputs, ∀ y, target.feasible (instanceMap x) y →
    source.feasible x (solutionMap x y)
  bounds : ∀ x ∈ sourceInputs, ∃ sourceOpt targetOpt : ℝ,
    IsOptimalValue source x sourceOpt ∧
    IsOptimalValue target (instanceMap x) targetOpt ∧
    targetOpt ≤ optimumFactor * sourceOpt ∧
    ∀ y, target.feasible (instanceMap x) y →
      |sourceOpt - source.value x (solutionMap x y)| ≤
        errorFactor * |targetOpt - target.value (instanceMap x) y|

end Lax213208.LReduction

concepts.title: Optimization problems
concepts.description:
An optimization problem specifies feasible solutions, nonnegative objective
values, and whether to minimize or maximize. Instances and solutions are
typed mathematical objects with fixed, injective representations.
Input size is the binary size of the instance's structural arena.

The predicates are relative to these representations. Input presentations
should come from the archive's structural combinators or certified
constructor derivations; injectivity alone does not exclude encoded advice.
concepts.sourceText:
import Mathlib.Data.NNReal.Basic
import Mathlib.Data.Set.Basic
import Lax560851.WordArena
import Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding

/-!
---
title: Optimization problems
type: definition
---
An optimization problem specifies feasible solutions, nonnegative objective
values, and whether to minimize or maximize. Instances and solutions are
typed mathematical objects with fixed, injective representations.
Input size is the binary size of the instance's structural arena.

The predicates are relative to these representations. Input presentations
should come from the archive's structural combinators or certified
constructor derivations; injectivity alone does not exclude encoded advice.
-/

namespace Lax213208.OptimizationProblem

open scoped NNReal
open Lax560851.StructuralPresentation Lax560851.WordArena
open Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding

inductive Direction
  | minimize
  | maximize

structure Problem (Instance Solution : Type*) where
  direction : Direction
  feasible : Instance → Solution → Prop
  value : Instance → Solution → ℝ≥0
  input : Presentation Instance
  output : Solution → List ℕ
  input_faithful : input.Faithful
  output_injective : Function.Injective output

variable {Instance Solution : Type*}

def inputWords (problem : Problem Instance Solution) (x : Instance) : List ℕ :=
  (encode problem.input x).toInput

def inputSize (problem : Problem Instance Solution) (x : Instance) : ℕ :=
  bitSize (inputWords problem x)

end Lax213208.OptimizationProblem

concepts.title: Polynomial-time maps
concepts.description:
A map is polynomial-time computable on a domain if one program returns its
encoded value within a polynomial resource bound in the encoded input size.
The encodings are fixed; no behavior is required outside the domain.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.Programs
import Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding

/-!
---
title: Polynomial-time maps
type: definition
---
A map is polynomial-time computable on a domain if one program returns its
encoded value within a polynomial resource bound in the encoded input size.
The encodings are fixed; no behavior is required outside the domain.
-/

namespace Lax213208.PolynomialComputation

open Programs Lax759944.BinaryWordEncoding

variable {Input Output : Type*}

def PolynomialTimeComputable (input : Input → List ℕ) (output : Output → List ℕ)
    (f : Input → Output) (domain : Set Input) : Prop :=
  ∃ alg : Program, ∃ c d : ℕ, 0 < c ∧ 0 < d ∧
    ∀ x ∈ domain,
      RunsWithin alg (input x) (output (f x)) (c * (bitSize (input x) + 2) ^ d)

end Lax213208.PolynomialComputation

concepts.title: Program execution
concepts.description:
We use the archive's word-RAM programs. An output is returned if it is
produced at every sufficiently large word width. This is an execution
relation, not a computability claim or a running-time bound.

A resource bound $T$ guarantees that input words and length fit in $T$ bits,
and that the same output is produced within $T$ instructions at every
width at least $T$. Lax62's compilation theorems establish the underlying
`ComputesInTime` judgment from high-level program specifications.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax808846.RamComputes
import Lax759944.RamPolytime

/-!
---
title: Program execution
type: definition
---
We use the archive's word-RAM programs. An output is returned if it is
produced at every sufficiently large word width. This is an execution
relation, not a computability claim or a running-time bound.

A resource bound $T$ guarantees that input words and length fit in $T$ bits,
and that the same output is produced within $T$ instructions at every
width at least $T$. Lax62's compilation theorems establish the underlying
`ComputesInTime` judgment from high-level program specifications.
-/

namespace Lax213208.Programs

open Lax808846.Ram Lax808846.RamComputes Lax759944.RamPolytime

abbrev Program := Lax808846.Ram.Program

def Returns (alg : Program) (input output : List ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ width : ℕ, ∀ w ≥ width, ∃ steps, RunsTo w alg input output steps

def RunsWithin (alg : Program) (input output : List ℕ) (bound : ℕ) : Prop :=
  FitsInWords bound (input.length :: input) ∧
    ∀ w ≥ bound, ComputesInTime w alg {input} (fun _ => output) (fun _ => bound)

end Lax213208.Programs

concepts.title: Polynomial-time approximation schemes
concepts.description:
A PTAS has approximation ratio $1+\varepsilon$ and polynomial running
time for every fixed $\varepsilon=1/k$, where $k$ is a positive integer.
One program handles all precisions.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.RApproximation
import Lax213208.RunningTime

/-!
---
title: Polynomial-time approximation schemes
type: definition
---
A PTAS has approximation ratio $1+\varepsilon$ and polynomial running
time for every fixed $\varepsilon=1/k$, where $k$ is a positive integer.
One program handles all precisions.
-/

namespace Lax213208.PTAS

open OptimizationProblem Programs RApproximation RunningTime

variable {Instance Solution : Type*} {problem : Problem Instance Solution}

def PTAS (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance) : Prop :=
  ∀ k : ℕ, 0 < k →
    let ε : ℝ := 1 / k
    Approximates (problem := problem) alg inputs (1 + ε) (some k) ∧
    PolynomialTime (problem := problem) alg inputs (some k)

end Lax213208.PTAS

concepts.title: Quasipolynomial-time approximation schemes
concepts.description:
A QPTAS has approximation ratio $1+\varepsilon$ and quasipolynomial
running time for every fixed $\varepsilon=1/k$, where $k$ is a positive integer.

concepts.title: Approximation guarantees
concepts.description:
A program approximates within $r\ge1$ if it returns a feasible
$r$-approximate solution on every instance in the class. This requires
termination, with no restriction on running time.

The optional integer precision selects the scheme input convention. Both ordinary
algorithms and schemes use this same predicate.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.Approximation
import Lax213208.AlgorithmInput
import Lax213208.Programs

/-!
---
title: Approximation guarantees
type: definition
---
A program approximates within $r\ge1$ if it returns a feasible
$r$-approximate solution on every instance in the class. This requires
termination, with no restriction on running time.

The optional integer precision selects the scheme input convention. Both ordinary
algorithms and schemes use this same predicate.
-/

namespace Lax213208.RApproximation

open OptimizationProblem Approximation AlgorithmInput Programs

variable {Instance Solution : Type*} {problem : Problem Instance Solution}

def Approximates (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance) (r : ℝ)
    (precision : Option ℕ := none) : Prop :=
  1 ≤ r ∧ ∀ x ∈ inputs, ∃ y,
    Returns alg (inputTape problem precision x) (problem.output y) ∧
    IsApproximation problem r x y

end Lax213208.RApproximation

concepts.title: Running time
concepts.description:
`RunsInTime alg inputs T` asserts termination within $T(n)$ instructions,
where $n$ is the binary size of the instance. The bound also supplies a
sufficient word width in bits. It says nothing about solution quality.

Polynomial, quasipolynomial, and subexponential time are independent of
approximation ratios. Subexponential time means $2^{o(n)}$: for every
$\delta>0$, a bound $c\,2^{\lceil\delta n\rceil}$ holds.
concepts.sourceText:
import Lax213208.AlgorithmInput
import Lax213208.Programs
import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Log
import Mathlib.Data.Real.Archimedean

/-!
---
title: Running time
type: definition
---
`RunsInTime alg inputs T` asserts termination within $T(n)$ instructions,
where $n$ is the binary size of the instance. The bound also supplies a
sufficient word width in bits. It says nothing about solution quality.

Polynomial, quasipolynomial, and subexponential time are independent of
approximation ratios. Subexponential time means $2^{o(n)}$: for every
$\delta>0$, a bound $c\,2^{\lceil\delta n\rceil}$ holds.
-/

namespace Lax213208.RunningTime

open OptimizationProblem AlgorithmInput Programs

variable {Instance Solution : Type*} {problem : Problem Instance Solution}

def RunsInTime (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance) (time : ℕ → ℕ)
    (precision : Option ℕ := none) : Prop :=
  ∀ x ∈ inputs, ∃ output,
    RunsWithin alg (inputTape problem precision x) output (time (inputSize problem x))

def PolynomialTime (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance)
    (precision : Option ℕ := none) : Prop :=
  ∃ c d : ℕ, 0 < c ∧ 0 < d ∧
    RunsInTime (problem := problem) alg inputs (fun n => c * (n + 2) ^ d) precision

def QuasipolynomialTime (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance)
    (precision : Option ℕ := none) : Prop :=
  ∃ c d : ℕ, 0 < c ∧ 0 < d ∧
    RunsInTime (problem := problem) alg inputs
      (fun n => 2 ^ (c * (Nat.log2 (n + 2) + 1) ^ d)) precision

def SubexponentialTime (alg : Program) (inputs : Set Instance)
    (precision : Option ℕ := none) : Prop :=
  ∀ δ : ℝ, 0 < δ → ∃ c : ℕ, 0 < c ∧
    RunsInTime (problem := problem) alg inputs (fun n => c * 2 ^ ⌈δ * n⌉₊) precision

end Lax213208.RunningTime
